name: Tangbe
blurb: The first village north of the Kagbeni checkpoint, on a shelf above the east bank of the Kali Gandaki. Whitewashed houses line narrow lanes, with apple orchards and buckwheat fields around them.

name: Chhusang
blurb: A spread-out village where the Narshing Khola joins the Kali Gandaki, facing cliffs pocked with old cave dwellings. Jeeps to and from Jomsom stop here, and it is the usual last night on the way out.

name: Chele
blurb: A small village on a ledge above the point where the Kali Gandaki flows out from under a huge block of red rock. The steep climb from the bridge marks the change from the valley floor to the high, dry ridge country beyond.
tip: Fill your bottles here; the climb towards Samar is dry and exposed to the sun from mid-morning.

name: Samar
blurb: A green pocket of poplars and irrigated fields in otherwise bare country, long used as a halt by horse and mule caravans. It is the usual lunch stop between Chele and Syangboche, with a view back to Nilgiri.

name: Yamda La
blurb: A cairn and prayer-flag saddle between Samar and Syangboche, the high point of the day from Chele. Published heights range from about 3,850 m to just over 4,000 m.

name: Syangboche
blurb: A handful of lodges in a hollow just below the Syangboche La, used as the second night north of Kagbeni. Not to be confused with Syangboche above Namche Bazaar in Khumbu.

name: Ghiling
blurb: A farming village set below the main trail in a broad side valley, with barley fields, poplars and an old red-walled monastery on the slope above the houses. It is a frequent overnight stop on the way back south.

name: Nyi La
blurb: The ridge that forms the southern boundary of Lo proper and, at about 4,010 m, the highest point of the walk in. The climb from the Ghiling side is long and gradual; the drop towards Ghami is shorter and steeper.

name: Ghami
blurb: One of the larger villages of Lo, a block of whitewashed houses above terraced fields. Just across the river on the way to Tsarang stands the longest mani wall in Mustang.

name: Tsarang La
blurb: A broad, windy saddle between Ghami and Tsarang, reached by a steady climb from the long mani wall. From the top the trail runs gently downhill for well over an hour to Tsarang. Also called the Choya La.

name: Tsarang
blurb: The second town of Lo, spread along a ridge above the Tsarang Khola canyon. A five-storey white dzong and a large red-walled monastery stand at its eastern end, and both can usually be visited for a fee.

name: Lo La
blurb: A notch in the last ridge before Lo Manthang, hung with prayer flags. It gives the first view of the walled town on its plain, about half an hour's walk below, with the hills of the Tibet border behind.

name: Lo Manthang
blurb: The walled capital of the former kingdom of Lo. Inside the earthen walls are the old royal palace and the Jampa, Thubchen and Chode temples, with wall paintings dating from the 15th century. Most lodges stand just outside the gate.
tip: One ticket from the monastery office normally covers the main temples; photography inside is not allowed.

name: Chhoser
blurb: A scatter of hamlets in the valley north-east of Lo Manthang, visited for the Jhong cave, a five-storey warren of rooms cut into a cliff, and the small Nyphu and Garphu monasteries built against the rock nearby.

name: Chogo La
blurb: The highest point of the usual Upper Mustang loop, on the western trail between Lo Manthang and Lo Gekar. A long, gradual climb over bare hills without water or shelter. Some maps call it the Marang La and give 4,230 m.

name: Lo Gekar
blurb: A small Nyingma monastery in a side valley west of Tsarang, better known as Ghar Gompa. Tradition says Guru Rinpoche founded it in the 8th century, before Samye in Tibet, which would make it one of the oldest Tibetan Buddhist temples anywhere.

name: Mui La
blurb: The second, lower pass of the day between Lo Gekar and Dhakmar. From the top the trail drops steeply through a gully in the red cliffs that give Dhakmar its name.

name: Dhakmar
blurb: A quiet village beneath fluted red cliffs riddled with old caves, away from the main jeep road. The name means red crag; legend puts the colour down to the blood of a demoness killed here by Guru Rinpoche.

name: Chungsi Cave
blurb: A cave shrine with natural rock formations revered as self-arisen chortens and linked to Guru Rinpoche. It lies deep in a canyon on the walking-only trail between Samar and Syangboche, well away from the jeep road.

name: Namgyal Gompa
blurb: A hilltop monastery about an hour's walk north-west of Lo Manthang; the name means monastery of victory. It makes a good half-day outing, with a view back over the walled town and its fields.

name: Yara
blurb: A village on the quieter east side of the Kali Gandaki, beneath cliffs eroded into organ-pipe flutes and dotted with old cave dwellings. It is the usual base for the walk to Luri Gompa.

name: Luri Gompa
blurb: A cave temple set high in a sandstone pinnacle about two hours' walk above Yara. Inside, a polished white chorten is surrounded by finely painted murals usually dated to the 13th or 14th century.
tip: The temple is kept locked; your guide needs to find the key-holder in the village below before you walk up.

name: Tangge
blurb: A compact village on the eastern return route, known for a group of large chortens painted in ochre, white and grey. The stage south from here to Tetang is the longest and driest day of the eastern loop.

name: Tetang
blurb: A fortified village of tall rammed-earth houses in the Narshing Khola valley, a short walk above Chhusang. Trekkers finishing the eastern loop pass through before crossing the Gyu La to Muktinath.

name: Gyu La
blurb: The pass on the foot trail between Tetang and Muktinath, an alternative way out of Upper Mustang that avoids the road down the Kali Gandaki. A long day with about 1,000 m of climbing and no water on the way.

name: Kora La
blurb: The pass on the Tibet border at the head of the valley, roughly 20 km beyond Lo Manthang by jeep track and one of the lowest crossings of the Himalayan divide. Visitors drive up for the view across the plateau when the road and the border police allow.
